title: Replicant Data — November 8, 2026: Business
lead: Maintenance, demonstration collection and integration change the economics of robot use.

news.title: Stretch's redesign makes maintenance a commercial feature
news.summary: Boston Dynamics redesigned its trailer-unloading robot around downtime causes found in earlier deployments. It promises faster module replacement, while the new version's economic effect still needs customer-site verification.
news.details: On November 3, Boston Dynamics introduced Stretch Gen 2, a new version of its mobile trailer-unloading robot. The company links the redesign to analysis of more than one hundred thousand operating hours from earlier machines. Updated connectors address vibration, the gripper has revised valves and sensing, and continuously rotating joints avoid earlier mechanical stops. The manufacturer says internal cabling was reduced by 81% to remove sources of wear and intermittent electrical faults.

news.limitations: Specifications are manufacturer claims. One thousand cases per hour depends on loads and stacking; the hundred thousand hours concern earlier machines, not the new version's proven lifespan.
news.evidence_status: Official manufacturer release; the new version's specifications are not confirmed by an independent comparative test.
news.body:
A loading dock purchases available working time as well as carton speed. If replacing a small component stops an otherwise capable system for an entire day, headline throughput no longer describes the shift's output. A new generation of warehouse equipment therefore needs assessment through maintenance access, spare parts and the customer's ability to perform repairs with its own technicians rather than always waiting for outside service.

On November 3, Boston Dynamics introduced Stretch Gen 2, a new version of its mobile trailer-unloading robot. Updated connectors address vibration, the gripper has revised valves and sensing, and continuously rotating joints avoid earlier mechanical stops. The manufacturer says internal cabling was reduced by 81% to remove sources of wear and intermittent electrical faults.

The company also reports replacing a drive module in about one hour rather than a full day. Advertised throughput reaches one thousand cases per hour but depends on case weight and stacking conditions; peak operation uses multiple-case picks. The battery is described as lasting two shifts, with charging to 90% taking around 75 minutes. These are the manufacturer's specifications and assessments, not an independent comparative warehouse evaluation of the new machine.

The announcement supplies no independent payback calculation. Customers need their own carton weights, shift schedules, downtime costs and module delivery times. The two-shift battery claim also needs a defined duration and duty cycle. Faster repair may be worth more than peak speed, but only if the service arrangement delivers the necessary part before a queue of unloaded trailers builds up.

news.title: Japan's AIRoA separates demonstration collection from robot availability
news.summary: AIRoA-0 learns from people using handheld grippers, so recording demonstrations does not require a robot fleet. The Japanese project reports 78% mean success on ten tasks, while transfer still depends on compatible tools and control integration.
news.details: AIRoA-0, described in a November 2 preprint, learns two-handed manipulation from 16,151 hours of human demonstrations. People record actions with YUBI handheld grippers without a robot at the recording site. Two wrist cameras supply images; the model estimates task progress and outputs gripper motions that each machine's controller converts into its own mechanical movements. The authors collected no demonstrations through remote human control of a robot and used neither learning through trials and rewards nor corrections performed on a robot.
news.technical_novelty: AIRoA-0, described in a November 2 preprint, learns two-handed manipulation from 16,151 hours of human demonstrations. People record actions with YUBI handheld grippers without a robot at the recording site. Two wrist cameras supply images; the model estimates task progress and outputs gripper motions that each machine's controller converts into its own mechanical movements. The authors collected no demonstrations through remote human control of a robot and used neither learning through trials and rewards nor corrections performed on a robot.
news.engineering_impact: Running identical weights on different platforms does not make integration free. Matching tools, camera placement and conversion into the particular robot's movements remain necessary. The developers describe adapting a new task in under four hours on eight H200 accelerators, a substantial computing node. Its cost belongs beside the robotic-cell time saved; this is not equivalent to changing a few settings on an ordinary laptop.
news.limitations: The 78% result covers ten Franka tasks. Other platforms require matching grippers, cameras and command conversion; independent replication is not established.
news.evidence_status: Preprint and author-conducted experiments; independent replication of these results is not established.
news.body:
A pilot budget often hides competition for the same machine: it is needed for collecting training examples, evaluation and useful production work. Japan's AIRoA association moves the first process outside the robotic cell. People record demonstrations with tools in their hands. That changes how examples can be collected, rather than eliminating demonstrator labor, quality control or the computing required to learn from the recordings.

AIRoA-0, described in a November 2 preprint, learns two-handed manipulation from 16,151 hours of human demonstrations. People record actions with YUBI handheld grippers without a robot at the recording site. Two wrist cameras supply images; the model estimates task progress and outputs gripper motions that each machine's controller converts into its own mechanical movements. The authors collected no demonstrations through remote human control of a robot and used neither learning through trials and rewards nor corrections performed on a robot.

On ten tasks using Franka hardware, the authors report 78% average success, compared with 27% for the strongest of four other models adapted using the same task demonstrations. Evaluation took place away from the training-recording locations. Examples include sorting parts, handling a pencil case and folding towels. The same weights also ran on TX-G2, OpenArm and UR with matching grippers. This does not establish the same 78% result on each of the four platforms.

Running identical weights on different platforms does not make integration free. Matching tools, camera placement and conversion into the particular robot's movements remain necessary. The developers describe adapting a new task in under four hours on eight H200 accelerators, a substantial computing node. Its cost belongs beside the robotic-cell time saved; this is not equivalent to changing a few settings on an ordinary laptop.

news.title: Caltech's orbital builder demonstrates an operation, not a finished service
news.summary: A Caltech robot assembled a new antenna-truss bay in orbit. Its maturity must be assessed alongside an incomplete structure, short communication windows and ground-team recovery work.
news.details: On November 5, Caltech reported an orbital ASTRA experiment, a robotic reflector-antenna assembly demonstration in NOM4D, a program investigating construction technologies for space, funded by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, DARPA. A manipulator takes tubes and connectors from dispensers, builds a bay on an assembly plate and pushes it outward. The intended antenna diameter is 1.4 meters. In orbit, two preassembled bays were extended and a third bay was assembled. The complete truss would contain eleven bays; the announcement does not report a finished antenna.

news.limitations: The antenna is unfinished. A ground team checks photographs and troubleshoots on a flight spare; communications are limited to short windows.
news.evidence_status: Caltech's account of its team's orbital demonstration; an independent assessment of the extent of autonomy is not supplied.
news.body:
Building in space could escape the size of a structure folded inside a launch vehicle's fairing. A potential future market and a demonstrated operation nevertheless represent different maturity levels. Caltech's announcement exposes an intermediate stage: components are genuinely joined in orbit while the team discovers how much engineering support unexpected situations require. Remote operation makes that support an especially visible part of the development process.

On November 5, Caltech reported an orbital ASTRA experiment, a robotic reflector-antenna assembly demonstration in NOM4D, a program investigating construction technologies for space, funded by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, DARPA. In orbit, two preassembled bays were extended and a third bay was assembled. The complete truss would contain eleven bays; the announcement does not report a finished antenna.

The ground team sent commands and checked the results in downloaded photographs. Communication is available during only seven or eight daily windows of roughly fifteen minutes. Unexpected problems were reproduced on a flight spare in the laboratory before a workaround was transmitted to the orbital machine. The team considers completion of the entire truss unlikely before the mission ends in December. Caltech presents the result as a proof of concept rather than a ready orbital construction service.

Building it, staffing the team and arranging limited communications would enter a future service cost. Assembly of a bay establishes a particular capability, but the announcement supplies no price for a completed antenna. news.title: HALO reduces demonstration recording while moving effort into simulation
news.summary: Apple demonstrated humanoid learning in generated homes followed by tests in six physical environments. Its 91% result covers 360 selected trials, and new kinds of work still require task design.
news.details: Apple researchers introduced HALO in a preprint submitted on November 4. Training episodes are generated in a thousand procedurally constructed homes: the pipeline synthesizes motion, places it in a scene and renders the robot's view. The resulting corpus contains 300 hours of synthetic episodes. During operation, a high-level module splits instructions into subtasks, a middle layer replans whole-body motion at about three updates per second, and a lower controller follows the plan at 50 hertz using depth and information about the robot's own mechanisms.
news.technical_novelty: Apple researchers introduced HALO in a preprint submitted on November 4. Training episodes are generated in a thousand procedurally constructed homes: the pipeline synthesizes motion, places it in a scene and renders the robot's view. The resulting corpus contains 300 hours of synthetic episodes. During operation, a high-level module splits instructions into subtasks, a middle layer replans whole-body motion at about three updates per second, and a lower controller follows the plan at 50 hertz using depth and information about the robot's own mechanisms.
news.engineering_impact: The particular operations in the evaluation matter to a customer. Sitting on a chair is different from providing home care, and pushing a box does not establish handling of fragile contents. The study identifies a concrete weakness: an object outside the camera's view supplies no direct contact signal. A pilot involving grasps hidden from the camera would need a dedicated evaluation of that condition.
news.limitations: New tasks require human-authored descriptions and keyframes. Vision supplies no direct signal for occluded contact; 91% applies to the selected 360 trials.
news.evidence_status: Preprint and author-conducted experiments; independent replication of these results is not established.
news.body:
Preparing examples without sending an operator to every target site changes early development economics. Virtual homes must still be generated, motions produced and checked, and models trained. The approach reduces dependence on manually recording every attempt but creates a different production chain with computing, verification and its own limits. A procurement comparison should account for that chain rather than interpreting synthetic data as a costless input.

Apple researchers introduced HALO in a preprint submitted on November 4. Training episodes are generated in a thousand procedurally constructed homes: the pipeline synthesizes motion, places it in a scene and renders the robot's view. The resulting corpus contains 300 hours of synthetic episodes. During operation, a high-level module splits instructions into subtasks, a middle layer replans whole-body motion at about three updates per second, and a lower controller follows the plan at 50 hertz using depth and information about the robot's own mechanisms.

The authors report 91% success across 360 trials in six physical environments that were neither used for training nor scanned beforehand. Demonstrations include sitting, passing sideways through doors, moving beneath tables and pushing boxes. Computation runs onboard. Adding a new task type still requires human-authored descriptions and keyframes, however, and vision provides no direct contact signal when an object becomes hidden.

The particular operations in the evaluation matter to a customer. Sitting on a chair is different from providing home care, and pushing a box does not establish handling of fragile contents. The study identifies a concrete weakness: an object outside the camera's view supplies no direct contact signal. A pilot involving grasps hidden from the camera would need a dedicated evaluation of that condition.

news.title: A humanoid's simulation score leaves a substantial integration gap
news.summary: HITCH links measured distances to commands for a humanoid's body parts. Researchers obtained a high score in one virtual benchmark, while physical box carrying succeeded in 13 of 20 attempts.
news.details: In a November 5 preprint, researchers from Tsinghua University, the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Qizhi Institute describe HITCH, a software harness for whole-body humanoid control. A model that processes images and language selects a point in an image and receives its three-dimensional position measured from depth. A separate interface accepts pelvis, torso, hand, walking and gaze commands. A planner turns these requests into coordinated references, and a learned controller follows them.
news.technical_novelty: In a November 5 preprint, researchers from Tsinghua University, the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Qizhi Institute describe HITCH, a software harness for whole-body humanoid control. A model that processes images and language selects a point in an image and receives its three-dimensional position measured from depth. A separate interface accepts pelvis, torso, hand, walking and gaze commands. A planner turns these requests into coordinated references, and a learned controller follows them.
news.engineering_impact: Thirty physical attempts cannot establish annual fleet availability or the cost of a successful operation. Successful carrying averaged 60.7 seconds including observation and motion. The remote server creates a local-network dependency, while operator judgment is different from automated acceptance. Before removing supervision, an integrator must specify how a box left in the wrong place will be detected and who owns that failure.
news.limitations: The 95% result is simulated; physical G1 evaluation covers two tasks using a remote server and operator judgment. The planner does not support sitting or stepping over obstacles.
news.evidence_status: Preprint and author-conducted experiments; independent replication of these results is not established.
news.organization: Tsinghua University; Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Shanghai Qizhi Institute
news.body:
Deployment requires separating the model's ability to choose a step from the machine's ability to execute it accurately. A control harness connects both levels and exposes integration work: depth measurements, body coordination, server execution, communications and outcome checking. A customer pilot has to assess those components together even when the supplier of the reasoning model can be changed independently of the rest of the equipment.

In a November 5 preprint, researchers from Tsinghua University, the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Qizhi Institute describe HITCH, a software harness for whole-body humanoid control. A model that processes images and language selects a point in an image and receives its three-dimensional position measured from depth. A separate interface accepts pelvis, torso, hand, walking and gaze commands. A planner turns these requests into coordinated references, and a learned controller follows them.

The model was trained on trajectories from five base tasks. Adding five demonstrations per task brought success on the simulated SIMPLE benchmark to 95%. Physical Unitree G1 tests had different outcomes: 13 successful carrying episodes out of 20 and six successful navigation episodes out of ten. The model ran on a remote server connected over Wi-Fi, with an operator judging the outcomes. Its training data contained no real images.

Thirty physical attempts cannot establish annual fleet availability or the cost of a successful operation. Successful carrying averaged 60.7 seconds including observation and motion. The remote server creates a local-network dependency, while operator judgment is different from automated acceptance. Before removing supervision, an integrator must specify how a box left in the wrong place will be detected and who owns that failure.
